section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department diplomatic correspondence and intelligence reports from late June through July 1941 (with one follow-up memorandum from April 1942) addressing the acute political crisis in Japan following the German invasion of the Soviet Union. The sudden German-Soviet hostilities shattered the assumptions underpinning Japan's alliance with Germany, prompting intense deliberations, the en bloc resignation of the second Konoye Cabinet on July 16, and the rapid formation of the third Konoye Cabinet under Prince Fumimaro Konoye on July 18. Diplomatic telegrams from Tokyo, Berlin, Rome, Moscow, and Shanghai analyze the strategic ouster of Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka, his replacement by Vice Admiral Teijiro Toyoda, Tokyo's public assertions of national self-reliance, and Japanese military preparations to occupy strategic bases in southern French Indochina. Accompanying reports from the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Consulate at Kobe document industrial conditions, critical raw material shortages, Japanese espionage practices, naval fleet movements, and stringent wartime port restrictions.

subfiles.about: Captain E. Jackson of the S.S. Clevendon reports on the Amagasaki electric plant, coal and food shortages in Japan, and Japanese naval intelligence operations disguised as ship repairs in Hong Kong.
subfiles.summary: Captain E. Jackson of the American steamship S.S. Clevendon provided intelligence to an FBI representative in Seattle based on his observations in Japan and the Far East in early 1940. He described the Amagasaki Japanese Government Electric Power Plant between Kobe and Osaka, highlighting its daily consumption of pulverized coal, high risk of spontaneous fires, and reliance on conscripted, malnourished workers. He also reported severe shortages of rice, leather, and municipal water in the Kobe-Osaka area due to military commandeering and maintenance deterioration. Jackson recounted an incident in Hong Kong where an allegedly damaged Japanese freighter served as a naval intelligence platform, warning that similar subterfuges might be attempted in American ports to spy on U.S. naval movements.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Intelligence Furnished by Captain E. Jackson Concerning Industrial and Strategic Conditions in Japan and Hong Kong

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on the convening of the Fourth Imperial Conference and statements issued by the Japanese Government and Foreign Minister Matsuoka regarding the German-Soviet war.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 920 reporting that the Fourth Imperial Conference since the start of the China Incident was held in the presence of the Emperor on July 2, 1941. The meeting was attended by Premier Konoye, senior cabinet ministers, and high-ranking military commanders from Imperial Headquarters. At 1:30 p.m., the government announced that a decision regarding fundamental national policy toward the current situation had been reached. Foreign Minister Matsuoka subsequently issued a public statement declaring that the German-Soviet war was more than an armed clash, warning that a 'super emergency period' was developing in the Far East, and urging the Japanese public to maintain coolness and unity.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 920 from Tokyo on the Fourth Imperial Conference and Foreign Minister Matsuoka's Statement

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew analyzes high-level Japanese policy debates revealing growing friction between German and Japanese conceptions of their new orders and press doubts regarding the Tripartite Pact.
subfiles.summary: In telegram No. 913 (sections 1 and 2), Ambassador Grew reports that high-level Japanese government deliberations reflect a deep conflict between Hitler's European New Order and Japan's Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere. Japanese dissatisfaction was provoked by the German Wohltat Economic Mission, which sought European trade with individual Far Eastern units without recognizing Japan's regional dominance. Articles in the newspaper Kokumin warned against Nazi socialism and noted that the German attack on the USSR placed the Tripartite Pact and the Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact into irreconcilable conflict, suggesting Japan might renounce one or both treaties. The embassy concludes that German economic and political expansion into Siberia and Asia poses an acknowledged danger to Japanese interests, weakening the foundation of the Tripartite alliance.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 913 from Tokyo on Strains in the Tripartite Alliance and Conflicting German and Japanese Ambitions

subfiles.about: Ambassador MacMurray reports confidential warnings from former Turkish Prime Minister Rauf Bey regarding Japanese Pan-Islamic intrigues in Iraq and Central Asia.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador MacMurray reports strictly confidential information from former Turkish Prime Minister Rauf Bey regarding Japanese efforts to extend political influence among Moslem populations. Rauf Bey believed that the recent revolt in Iraq was engineered by a Japanese commercial mission and revealed that Japanese agents had approached him years earlier, and again recently, through a Turcoman named Hodjare Shidpra (Reshid) and Japanese diplomats in Ankara. The agents sought to enlist his leadership in creating an autonomous Turcoman state in Chinese and Russian Turkestan. Rauf Bey warned that this pro-Japanese movement claimed 500,000 adherents among Moslems in British and Dutch colonial possessions, maintaining complex and confusing relationships with communist activities.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Ankara regarding Japanese Subversive and Pan-Islamic Activities in the Middle East and Central Asia

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reviews Tokyo newspaper editorials reacting to the July 2 Imperial Conference, emphasizing national self-reliance, unity, and resolution of the China Incident.
subfiles.summary: In telegram No. 927 (sections 1 and 2), Ambassador Grew summarizes Japanese press reactions to the July 2 Imperial Conference. Editorials generally adhered to government secrecy while echoing Matsuoka's call for unity, sacrifice, and immediate domestic preparation. Hochi asserted that Japan could no longer count on benefits from its Axis allies and must rely strictly on its own national power, while Miyako argued that British and American aid to Chiang Kai-shek must be halted, predicting that Japan might eventually be forced to use military force against powers blocking its southward advance. Nichi Nichi, Yomiuri, and Kokumin questioned whether the nation's internal structure was ready for an unprecedented crisis and urged the cabinet to act without error.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 927 from Tokyo on Japanese Press Reactions to the Imperial Conference Decisions

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on Prime Minister Konoye's national radio address on East Asia Day emphasizing national perseverance, patriotism, and self-sufficiency.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 919 detailing Prime Minister Konoye's radio broadcast to the nation on July 1 (East Asia Day) in his capacity as President of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association. Konoye praised the resilience of the Japanese people through five years of conflict and acknowledged the economic inconveniences and material shortages facing civilians. He declared that Japan was advancing toward economic self-sufficiency by acquiring essential resources from East Asia rather than relying on outside imports. Emphasizing that 'Japan must follow the path of Japan' regardless of shifting world events, the Premier appealed for unbreakable national unity and loyalty to Japan's destiny.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 919 from Tokyo on Prime Minister Konoye's East Asia Day Radio Address

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on press commentary regarding frequent private meetings between Premier Konoye and Marquis Kido, Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 969 citing a special article in the newspaper Kokumin concerning frequent conferences between Prime Minister Konoye and Marquis Koichi Kido, Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal. The press and diplomatic corps viewed these discussions as having high political significance given the prominent status of both figures. While noting that Konoye enjoyed public confidence and Foreign Minister Matsuoka had attained peak popularity following his European trip, the article expressed public curiosity about whether these high-level talks presaged an impending renovation of national policy.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 969 from Tokyo on Speculation Concerning Frequent Conferences Between Konoye and Kido

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew sends an urgent triple-priority telegram reporting that the entire Japanese Cabinet resigned en bloc.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew sends telegram No. 1014 under urgent triple-priority marking at midnight on July 16, 1941. The brief message reports that the entire Japanese Cabinet resigned en bloc tonight. No details regarding the causes or prospective successors were included in this initial announcement.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1014 from Tokyo on the Resignation of the Japanese Cabinet En Bloc

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew sends a rush telegram confirming that Prince Fumimaro Konoye will head the newly formed Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits rush telegram No. 1019 informing the Department of State that Prince Fumimaro Konoye will head the new Japanese Cabinet. The report confirms that Konoye received the imperial command following the en bloc resignation of his previous administration.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1019 from Tokyo announcing Konoye to Head New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew details the conference of senior statesmen (Jushin) that recommended Konoye to form a new cabinet and the resignations of top administrative officials.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports in telegram No. 1022 that a conference of senior statesmen (Jushin) was convened at the Imperial Palace on July 17, attended by Marquis Kido, Yoshimichi Hara, Reijiro Wakatsuki, Keisuke Okada, Koki Hirota, Senjuro Hayashi, Nobuyuki Abe, and Mitsumasa Yonai. Following the conference, Marquis Kido reported to the Emperor, who commanded Prince Konoye to form a new cabinet. Simultaneously, Prime Minister Konoye requested and received the resignations of Cabinet Advisory Council members, including Fusanosuke Kuhara. Resignations were likewise submitted by vice ministers, Chief Cabinet Secretary Tomita, Information Board officials, Police Bureau Director Hashimoto, Metropolitan Police Chief Yamazaki, and Imperial Rule Assistance Association Vice President Yanagawa.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1022 from Tokyo on the Senior Statesmen Conference and Resignations of Key Officials

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits the official statement of the Board of Information explaining the Cabinet's en bloc resignation.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 1016 containing the official text released by the Board of Information regarding the cabinet's resignation en bloc. The statement explained that the cabinet, installed the previous summer, recognized the necessity of strengthening the internal structure to execute national policy vigorously amid rapid international changes, requiring sweeping cabinet reforms. Premier Konoye assembled the resignations of his ministers at a special cabinet meeting and traveled to the Hayama Imperial Villa at 9 p.m. to present them to the Emperor. His Majesty instructed Konoye to continue managing state affairs until further notice.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1016 from Tokyo transmitting Board of Information Statement on Cabinet Resignation

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the ministerial lineup of the third Konoye Cabinet, including Vice Admiral Teijiro Toyoda as Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew sends rush telegram No. 1029 announcing the official composition of the third Konoye Cabinet. Prince Fumimaro Konoye serves as Prime Minister and concurrently Minister of Justice, while Vice Admiral Teijiro Toyoda takes Foreign Affairs concurrently with Overseas Affairs. Tojo remains Minister of War, Oikawa stays as Minister of the Navy, and Hiranuma, Yanagawa, and Planning Board President Suzuki serve as Ministers without Portfolio. Sakonji is appointed to Commerce, Ogura to Finance, Hashida to Education, Ino to Agriculture, Tanabe to Home Affairs, Murata to Railways, and Koizumi to Welfare.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1029 from Tokyo announcing Personnel of the Third Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew provides a biographical sketch and diplomatic appraisal of Vice Admiral Teijiro Toyoda, the newly appointed Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 1030 evaluating Vice Admiral Teijiro Toyoda upon his appointment as Minister for Foreign Affairs. Prior to assuming Commerce on April 4, Toyoda served as Vice Minister of the Navy and Chief of the Bureau of Aeronautics, having twice served at the Japanese Embassy in London, including as Naval Attaché in 1923. According to the U.S. Naval Attaché, Toyoda has an outstanding service reputation as an administrator, possesses no pro-Axis leanings, speaks good English, and is frank, communicative, and friendly toward the United States and Great Britain. Genuine regret was voiced in Japanese naval circles when he retired to accept ministerial appointments, and he retains warm relations with American and British naval officers, notably Captain F. F. Rogers, USN.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1030 from Tokyo assessing Background and Outlook of Foreign Minister Teijiro Toyoda

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on press reactions under censorship constraints, Konoye's conferences with Hiranuma and service ministers, and the political sidelining of Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: In telegram No. 1024 (sections 1 and 2), Ambassador Grew reports that strict press censorship prohibited speculation regarding cabinet candidates, restricting newspapers to general hopes for a strong, unified ministry capable of executing national policy. Following his imperial audience, Premier Konoye conferred for 50 minutes with Baron Hiranuma, followed by visits from the Army and Navy Ministers, indicating that Hiranuma remains a decisive political force. Hiranuma also met with his close associate Kazami (Kozoota), former Chief Cabinet Secretary. Former Foreign Minister Matsuoka was reported ill and absent from public sessions since July 10, skipping the decisive resignation meetings, though he had attended a private banquet on July 15.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1024 from Tokyo on Cabinet Reorganization Developments and Political Maneuvers

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew provides a confidential analysis attributing the Cabinet collapse to German-Soviet hostilities, Hiranuma's insistence on ministerial responsibility, and Konoye's desire to drop Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits strictly confidential telegram No. 1025 analyzing the structural causes of the cabinet change. The unexpected German assault on the Soviet Union shattered the fundamental premise of Japan's alliance with Germany, creating insurmountable difficulties for the cabinet. Baron Hiranuma, whose own ministry fell after the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact, insisted that ministers must assume responsibility when their miscalculations cause anxiety to the Emperor. Furthermore, deep policy rifts existed between Premier Konoye and Foreign Minister Matsuoka, particularly regarding Matsuoka's interpretation of Article III of the Tripartite Pact that Japan must side with Germany in a conflict with the United States. Resignation en bloc was deliberately used as a constitutional device to purge Matsuoka without requiring imperial dismissal.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1025 from Tokyo analyzing Underlying Causes of the Cabinet Crisis and Matsuoka's Ouster

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the resignations of Ambassador to Nanking Kumataro Honda and Foreign Vice Minister Chuichi Ohashi following the cabinet shakeup.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 1033 stating that according to press reports, Kumataro Honda, Japanese Ambassador to the Nanking regime, and Chuichi Ohashi, Foreign Vice Minister, submitted their resignations today. The departures reflect the bureaucratic and diplomatic fallout from the removal of Foreign Minister Matsuoka.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1033 from Tokyo on the Resignations of Ambassador Honda and Vice Minister Ohashi

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits public statements by Prince Konoye and War Minister Tojo affirming that national policy remains fixed and immutable while urging swift consolidation of the wartime structure.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports in telegram No. 1034 that the press published statements by Prime Minister Konoye and War Minister Tojo. Konoye emphasized that Japan's policy had been fixed but required decisive speed in execution, demanding the rapid consolidation of the domestic structure. General Tojo declared that government policy remained immutable regardless of the cabinet change and appealed for complete unity among all government and military organs to expedite the wartime structure and integrate political and military measures.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1034 from Tokyo transmitting Statements by Premier Konoye and War Minister Tojo

subfiles.about: Chargé Leland Morris reports on subdued German reactions in Berlin to the Tokyo cabinet shakeup and Germany's concern over Far Eastern policy.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Morris transmits telegram No. 2901 reporting that the Berlin press covered the Japanese cabinet change with front-page placement but subdued prominence. The semi-official Dienst aus Deutschland affirmed that Berlin circles believed the new Japanese government remained fully committed to the Three Power Pact, claiming Germany was kept closely informed and welcomed Japan's freedom from internal checks. Morris observes that this belated and unenthusiastic commentary suggests Berlin's hopes for an immediate Japanese military diversion against Soviet Russia in the Far East have receded, leaving German officials to console themselves with the belief that Tokyo's Axis alignment will not be abandoned.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 2901 from Berlin on German Press and Official Reactions to the Japanese Cabinet Changes

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on a national radio address by Information Board President Nobufumi Ito urging Japan to depend solely on its own strength.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports in telegram No. 1036 on a nationwide radio address by Nobufumi Ito, President of the Board of Information. Ito reiterated that the cabinet reorganization was designed to consolidate the domestic front in response to a constantly changing international scene. Reviewing European events since the fall of France, he discussed Britain's efforts to reach an agreement with Russia, questioned the solidarity of the Anglo-Soviet and American-Soviet partnerships, and characterized the conflict as too complex to be viewed as a simple ideological war. He concluded that Japan must not rely on any other nation and must fulfill its national ideals based strictly on objective reality and its own power.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1036 from Tokyo on Information Board Chief Ito's Radio Address on Self-Reliance

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports a Yomiuri editorial emphasizing that the fundamental foreign policy formulated at the Imperial Conference remains unaltered.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 1037 summarizing an editorial in Yomiuri regarding the diplomacy of the third Konoye Cabinet. The paper asserted that the national policy decided at the Imperial Conference of July 2 remained entirely intact, explaining that variations in diplomatic tone, method, and form did not indicate a fundamental shift. Yomiuri exhorted the public to recognize their responsibilities in a volatile world and remember Premier Konoye's broadcast declaration that Japan must depend solely upon its own strength.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1037 from Tokyo on Yomiuri Editorial on Foreign Policy Continuity and Self-Reliance

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew provides a comprehensive four-part assessment of the third Konoye Cabinet, Tokyo press reactions, the Konoye-Hiranuma axis, and the diplomatic impact of Matsuoka's removal.
subfiles.summary: In telegram No. 1035 (sections 1 through 4), Ambassador Grew analyzes the reception and composition of the third Konoye Cabinet. The Japanese press acclaimed its rapid formation, strong military representation, and exclusion of party politicians, viewing it as a reorganization rather than a governmental collapse. Commentators identified a dominant Konoye-Hiranuma axis, with Baron Hiranuma functioning as virtual Vice Premier, while new Foreign Minister Toyoda emphasized diplomatic flexibility rather than slavish adherence to foreign systems. Financial circles welcomed Masatsune Ogura's appointment to Finance, anticipating close cooperation with Suzuki and Sakonji. Grew concludes that Matsuoka's eclipse eliminates a pro-Nazi influence fundamentally unacceptable to Japan, providing a unified administration that is less likely to follow German dictates or precipitate a clash with the United States.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1035 from Tokyo on Political Composition and Significance of the Third Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: Consul General Lockhart summarizes Shanghai press reactions across English-language, Japanese, and Chinese newspapers concerning the new Tokyo cabinet and Matsuoka's ouster.
subfiles.summary: In telegram No. 900 (sections 1 and 2), Consul General Lockhart summarizes Shanghai press commentary on the Japanese cabinet reconstruction. English-language journals, including the Shanghai Evening Post, North China Daily News, The China Press, and Shanghai Times, viewed the reorganization as primarily designed to remove the reckless and talkative Matsuoka, describing Toyoda as an intelligent moderate who might pursue a cautious waiting policy while avoiding conflict with Anglo-Saxon powers, though an advance into French Indochina remained possible. Japanese and Nanking-controlled papers warned that Western powers would be deceived if they expected Japan to abandon the Axis, while pro-Chungking Chinese papers interpreted Toyoda's appointment as an attempt to seek rapprochement with Washington, urging the United States not to be misled.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 900 from Shanghai on Local Press Reactions to the Japanese Cabinet Shakeup

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew summarizes Tokyo press editorials on the need for independent diplomacy and media criticism of Foreign Office officials resigning out of loyalty to Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reviews editorial comment from Hochi, Miyako, Kokumin, and Chugai in telegram No. 1043. Hochi noted that the German blitzkrieg against Russia altered the fundamental premise of Japan's diplomacy, while Miyako argued that recent history demonstrated security cannot be secured through international treaties, requiring Japan to pursue fully independent diplomacy. Kokumin strongly criticized the resignations of Ambassador Honda, Vice Minister Ohashi, and advisors Saito and Shiratori, condemning the feudal concept of following Matsuoka into 'martyrdom' as out of step with national interests. Chugai criticized the elaborate farewell demonstration staged for Matsuoka by Foreign Office personnel as inappropriate in wartime and inconsiderate toward the incoming Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1043 from Tokyo reviewing Press Commentary on Foreign Policy Independence and Resignations

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits Tokyo press editorials advocating flexible diplomacy to adapt to the German-Soviet conflict while settling the China incident.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 1049 summarizing commentary from Asahi, Miyako, and Chugai regarding the third Konoye Cabinet's diplomacy. Asahi argued that while basic national policy was unchanged, diplomatic measures must be varied and flexible to cope with global disruptions caused by the German-Soviet conflict, urging that diplomacy be concentrated on settling the China Incident. Miyako asserted that personnel harmony achieved in the new ministry would provide strong authority to execute an independent foreign policy, while Chugai expressed gratification that foreign commentators correctly understood that the cabinet reconstruction did not signify an alteration of Japan's foreign policy goals.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1049 from Tokyo reviewing Press Calls for Diplomatic Flexibility

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew presents an in-depth analysis of the growing Japanese estrangement from Nazi Germany, German arrogance in Tokyo, and the prospects for Japan's foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: In telegram No. 1052 (sections 1 and 2, along with its official State Department paraphrase on page 218), Ambassador Grew provides a comprehensive assessment of the strategic forces behind the cabinet crisis. Grew deduces that Japan is increasingly dissatisfied with its subordinate role in the Axis alliance, noting that while the unannounced German invasion of Russia precipitated the crisis, long-term resentment had been provoked by German arrogance, racial contempt for the Japanese, intrusive Gestapo activities in Tokyo, and German Ambassador Ott's overbearing attempts to regiment the Japanese press. Baron Hiranuma forced the cabinet's resignation on the constitutional principle that ministers must accept responsibility for failing to anticipate the German attack. Grew predicts no sudden volte-face away from the Tripartite Pact, but observes that dropping Matsuoka—dismissively called 'Hitler's office boy'—enables Tokyo to pursue an independent foreign policy and could eventually lead to gradual rapprochement with Anglo-American nations.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1052 and Paraphrase from Tokyo analyzing Japanese Disillusionment with the Axis and Future Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: Ambassador Phillips reports on the subdued and cautious coverage of the Japanese Cabinet changes in the Italian press.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Phillips transmits telegram No. 1072 reporting that Italian newspapers provided surprisingly sparse and reserved coverage of the Japanese cabinet crisis. Dispatches briefly depicted the government changes as proof of Tokyo's continued loyalty to the Tripartite Pact while largely ignoring the political fall of Matsuoka, whose name was scarcely mentioned. Italian editorial writers preferred to discuss Lord Halifax's speech and American policy rather than the cabinet shakeup. Virginio Gayda in Il Giornale d'Italia remarked cautiously that it was impossible to appraise the Japanese situation until the new cabinet was fully formed, with commentators refraining from predicting Japan's future course.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1072 from Rome on Italian Press Reactions to the Japanese Cabinet Crisis

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports Japanese press coverage highlighting Foreign Minister Toyoda's assurances to German and Italian ambassadors that foreign policy remains anchored in the Tripartite Pact.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports in telegram No. 1053 that Tokyo newspapers carried leading articles emphasizing that the foundation of Japanese foreign policy remained firmly rooted in the Tripartite Pact. The press highlighted Foreign Minister Toyoda's conferences on July 19 with the German and Italian ambassadors, where he officially assured them that Japan's diplomacy was unchanged. Press commentaries noted that policy toward China remained focused on strengthening the Nanking government, asserting that Ambassador Honda's continuation in office disproved Chungking propaganda. Editorials in Hochi and Kokumin criticized Western interpretations that Japan's declarations of self-reliance indicated a shift away from the Axis, insisting Toyoda's statements should clarify Tokyo's unwavering alignment.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1053 from Tokyo on Diplomatic Assurances to Axis Ambassadors and Policy Toward China

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits an exchange of official messages between Prime Minister Konoye and Wang Ching-wei reaffirming Sino-Japanese collaboration.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 1062 reporting an exchange of official messages between Prime Minister Konoye and Wang Ching-wei, President of the Nanking regime. Konoye affirmed that the cabinet change was intended solely to strengthen Japan's domestic execution of policy, assuring Wang that Japan's policy toward Nanking and their mutual collaboration would remain completely unaffected. In response, Wang congratulated Konoye on forming his third cabinet, expressing enhanced self-confidence from their recent personal meetings in Tokyo and pledging joint efforts on the basis of immutable policies to achieve the stabilization and prosperity of East Asia.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1062 from Tokyo on Exchange of Messages Between Premier Konoye and Wang Ching-wei

subfiles.about: Ambassador Steinhardt reports a confidential conversation with Japanese Ambassador Yoshitsugu Tatekawa regarding Indochina, Matsuoka's ouster, and the German military advance in Russia.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Steinhardt transmits strictly confidential telegram No. 1402 recounting a conversation with Japanese Ambassador to the Soviet Union Yoshitsugu Tatekawa. Tatekawa attributed the ouster of Foreign Minister Matsuoka primarily to personal jealousy within the Japanese government. He indicated that Japan's military move into French Indochina was proceeding with the full agreement of the Vichy Government, albeit under pressure, while any Japanese military action against the Soviet Union remained on hold. Tatekawa also believed that the German army was clearing Soviet forces in its rear and would launch a major drive against Leningrad, Moscow, and Kiev within ten days, noting that most of the Soviet government had already evacuated Moscow.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1402 from Moscow on Ambassador Tatekawa's Views on Japanese Moves and the Soviet Front

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports a Kokumin article discussing historical precedents for the military high command taking the initiative when government policy becomes stagnant.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports in telegram No. 1081 on a special article in Kokumin analyzing relations between the Japanese government and the military high command. The paper observed that while civilian policy makers led during the Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese wars, political leadership was unprepared when the Manchurian and China incidents broke out, forcing the military high command to take the initiative. Given the current international crisis, Kokumin urged the government to act positively and forcefully first, warning that failure to do so would destroy complete unity between the civilian administration and the armed forces.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1081 from Tokyo on Kokumin Article Regarding Government Policy and Military Initiative

subfiles.about: Consul Butrick reports political intelligence provided by Dr. J. Leighton Stuart concerning internal Japanese dissension, General Ugaki, and military disputes between Tojo and Itagaki.
subfiles.summary: Consul Butrick transmits strictly confidential telegram No. 183 conveying intelligence provided by Dr. J. Leighton Stuart, President of Yenching University, based on high-level Chinese contacts. Stuart reported that General Kazushige Ugaki was considered for Prime Minister during the cabinet reorganization, but liberal elements supporting him were not strong enough to secure control, while Matsuoka was dropped to provide greater diplomatic flexibility. Stuart reported deep dissension within Japan, including an altercation between War Minister Tojo and General Seishiro Itagaki over Itagaki's unauthorized negotiations with Chiang Kai-shek, which prompted complaints from Wang Ching-wei and led to Itagaki's transfer from Central China to Korea. Stuart reiterated his conviction that the United States could best serve its interests and those of Japanese liberals by providing strong assistance to China.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 183 from Peiping transmitting Leighton Stuart's Insights on Japanese Leadership and Dissension

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the official appointment of Michiyo Iwamura as Minister of Justice in the third Konoye Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports in telegram No. 1086 that special newspaper editions announced the appointment of Michiyo Iwamura as Minister of Justice. Iwamura, who had served as Vice Minister of Justice and Chief Procurator General, relieves Prime Minister Konoye of his concurrent holding of the Justice portfolio.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1086 from Tokyo announcing Appointment of Michiyo Iwamura as Justice Minister

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew relays a report from Consul Warner in Kobe detailing travel delays for British couriers, police surveillance of foreigners, and substantial Japanese naval movements in Bungo Strait.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 1069 forwarding a message from Consul Warner in Kobe dated July 23. Warner reported heightened security measures, including military police restrictions on train reservations that delayed British Embassy couriers, alongside systematic police logging of persons visiting the Kobe Club. Axis merchant vessels were being repainted gray, with the exception of the German vessel Scharnhorst and three Hamburg-American Line ships, while the Italian warship Eritrea underwent renovation. Warner also reported that on July 21 the merchant vessel Tjisaroa encountered a major Japanese naval detachment in Bungo Strait south of Shikoku, comprising 23 submarines, 3 cruisers, and 2 aircraft carriers proceeding north, amid extensive military shipping activity in Osaka Bay.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1069 from Tokyo transmitting Kobe Report on Courier Restrictions, Police Surveillance, and Naval Activity

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew comments on the Kokumin article as evidence that the military high command may have coerced the civilian government into the occupation of Indochina bases.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits telegram No. 1090 referring to the Kokumin article reported in his telegram No. 1081. Grew notes that he considers the newspaper article highly significant as an indication that the military high command may have forced the hand of the government regarding the execution of plans to occupy military bases in French Indochina.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1090 from Tokyo on Military High Command Forcing Policy on French Indochina

subfiles.about: The Acting Secretary of State informs Ambassador Grew that intelligence indicates the move into Indochina was methodically planned with full cooperation between civilian and military authorities.
subfiles.summary: In telegram No. 441, the Acting Secretary of State replies to Ambassador Grew's telegram No. 1090 concerning the Japanese occupation of Indochina bases. Intelligence from diverse sources indicates that the Japanese advance was methodically planned with complete cooperation between the armed services and the civilian branch of the Japanese government. While acknowledging that original initiative may have come from the military high command, the State Department concludes that the Japanese government as a whole has favored the Indochina move for some time.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 441 to Tokyo regarding Government-Military Accord on Indochina Move

subfiles.about: FBI Director Hoover transmits a confidential intelligence memorandum describing hydroelectric dams, railway traffic, aircraft factories, and arsenals across the Japanese Empire.
subfiles.summary: FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover transmits a letter and memorandum to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr., detailing confidential intelligence regarding strategic infrastructure and industrial facilities in Japan, Korea, and Manchuria. The report describes the Suiho Dam on the Yalu River, noting its dimensions, 400,000 kW generator capacity, and power transmission to Korean cement plants, alongside traffic assessments for the South Manchurian and Trans-Siberian railways and shortages of cotton and peanuts. In Japan proper, the report details the Mitsubishi aircraft plant in Nagoya (noting presence of 60 German engineers, plane output, and 55 arrests for sabotage), a large tank arsenal extending five miles along Uchiura Bay in Hokkaido, hill fortifications at Otaru, scrap iron reserves at the Yawata Iron Works in Kokura, and branch factories of the Tachizawa Iron Works in Osaka and Okayama prefectures.
subfiles.title: FBI Letter and Intelligence Memorandum on Industrial, Power, and Military Installations in Japan, Korea, and Manchuria

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits Consul Warner's report from Kobe detailing dock entry pass restrictions on American President Lines personnel, heavy troop departures, and blocked Dutch funds.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew conveys telegram No. 1119 (accompanied by its official paraphrase on page 239) forwarding a dispatch of July 25 from Consul Warner at Kobe. Warner reported that Japanese authorities refused general dock passes with photographs to foreign and Japanese employees of the American President Lines, permitting only individual passes for specific ships. Exceptionally heavy westbound railway traffic was observed, along with an average of eight freighters (including troop transports) departing Osaka Bay daily, and the departure of the merchant ship Tjisaroa for Yokohama with a compulsory Japanese pilot. Furthermore, the Netherlands Consul General reported that roughly ten million guilders were immobilized in cotton goods awaiting export permits withheld by Japanese authorities.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1119 and Paraphrase from Tokyo transmitting Kobe Report on Port Restrictions, Troop Shipments, and Blocked Funds

subfiles.about: State Department official Schmidt records a telephone inquiry from maritime attorney Paul H. Lacques regarding the specific dates the port of Kobe was closed to foreign shipping in the summer of 1941 prior to asset-freezing orders.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Schmidt of the State Department records a telephone conversation with Paul H. Lacques of the New York law firm Bigham, Englar, Jones and Houston. Mr. Lacques inquired whether the Department possessed official information confirming the specific dates the port of Kobe was closed to foreigners during the spring and summer of 1941, noting a New York Times report that the port had been closed for ten days in July 1941 prior to the July 28 freezing regulations. Schmidt replied that while he was personally aware that sections of Kobe port and certain piers had been periodically closed to foreigners, he could not provide exact dates on the spot, but promised to review departmental records and telegraph the requested information to Lacques at his firm's expense.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Paul H. Lacques and Mr. Schmidt regarding Dates of Closure of the Port of Kobe
